speaker: Bob Mumgaard
title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems' Bob Mumgaard on fusion tech (#1171)
question: In magnetic confinement fusion, how much stronger do magnets need to be to unlock dramatically smaller tokamaks?
guest: In these machines, we have built so many of them that we understand them well enough to know that the performance scales roughly as the magnetic field to the fourth power, so there is a huge lever on it. Even with a factor of two, you are talking about a factor of 16 on the other side. So we are aiming for just a factor of two, which was granted a factor of two beyond what people had been working on for a long time, but a new material allowed us to do that.

points.note: Accept: 2x magnetic field yields ~16x gain (or dramatically smaller reactor volume), showing a 10x or 100x magnet leap is unnecessary. Do not credit: guessing 10x/100x stronger magnets are required or omitting the ~2x threshold.

points.core: New superconducting materials unlocked that previously unreachable factor-of-two magnetic field jump.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Roughly a doubling of field strength is enough. Fusion power density in a tokamak scales approximately with the fourth power of the magnetic field (at fixed plasma beta), so doubling the field boosts power per unit volume about 16-fold, which lets you shrink the plasma volume by an order of magnitude or more for the same output.

The concrete comparison is ITER versus SPARC. ITER uses low-temperature niobium-tin superconductors, giving about 5.3 tesla at the plasma centre (around 12 T peak at the coil). Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT's SPARC uses high-temperature superconducting (REBCO) tape, targeting about 12.2 T on axis and roughly 20 T at the coil, a field level demonstrated in their 2021 large-bore test magnet. With that roughly 2x field increase, SPARC aims for net energy gain (Q > 1, possibly Q ≈ 10) in a device with a major radius of 1.85 m versus ITER's 6.2 m, which is about 40 times smaller in plasma volume.

The practical limits then shift from the superconductor to structural stresses on the magnet and heat exhaust at the walls, both of which become harder as the machine shrinks.

models.answer: Roughly doubling the magnetic field in the plasma—enabled by making the magnets themselves about 1.6 to 2 times stronger—is enough to shrink a tokamak dramatically. Because fusion power density scales with the fourth power of the magnetic field ($B^4$), doubling field strength increases fusion power per unit volume sixteenfold while also improving energy confinement. Conventional low-temperature superconductors, like ITER’s niobium-tin magnets, hit practical limits around 12 to 13 tesla at the coil, producing 5.3 tesla at the plasma center and requiring an 840-cubic-meter plasma chamber. High-temperature superconductors made with rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) push peak coil fields to roughly 20 tesla and on-axis plasma fields past 12 tesla. That roughly twofold jump in plasma field lets compact designs like Commonwealth Fusion Systems’ SPARC target net fusion energy at about one-fortieth of ITER’s plasma volume and less than a third of its major radius.

Roughly **doubling** the magnetic field strength is enough to unlock dramatically smaller tokamaks. Conventional low-temperature superconducting designs like ITER max out near 12 to 13 tesla at the magnet coils, producing about 5.3 tesla at the plasma center. Newer high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets made with rare-earth barium copper oxide tape push peak coil fields past 20 tesla, raising the central plasma field to around 12 tesla.

That ~2x jump in field strength produces an outsized reduction in reactor size because tokamak physics scales steeply with magnetic field. At a fixed plasma stability limit, fusion power density scales with the fourth power of the magnetic field ($B^4$), meaning a doubled field yields sixteen times more fusion power per cubic meter. Stronger fields also shrink ion gyro-orbits, substantially improving energy confinement. Together, these effects allow compact HTS designs like SPARC to target net fusion energy in a plasma volume roughly 40 to 60 times smaller than ITER's.

Roughly **twice as strong**. Fusion power density at fixed plasma pressure ratio (beta) scales with about the **fourth power** of the magnetic field. Doubling the field therefore gives about **16 times** the power density. In principle, that lets a device make the same fusion power with about one-sixteenth of the plasma volume. Confinement also improves with field, so you can reach high gain at a much smaller size.

The best-known example is Commonwealth Fusion Systems' SPARC. It uses high-temperature superconducting (REBCO) magnets that reach about **20 tesla at the coil** and about **12 tesla on the plasma axis**. ITER's older niobium-tin magnets give about **5.3 tesla** on axis. That makes SPARC's field a bit more than twice ITER's. As a result, SPARC's major radius is about 1.85 meters versus ITER's 6.2 meters, and its plasma volume is roughly **1/40th** of ITER's. It still targets a fusion gain (Q) above 1, with simulations predicting around 10.

So the field needs to roughly double, from about 5 to 6 tesla on axis to about 12 tesla, which means coil fields of about 20 tesla. These numbers come from well-established tokamak scaling and published SPARC and ITER design figures. I didn't run a search to re-check them for this answer.

Magnets only need to be about two to three times stronger than conventional superconducting magnets to shrink tokamaks dramatically. This is because fusion power density scales roughly with the fourth power of the magnetic field strength, while the plasma volume needed for comparable fusion performance shrinks roughly with the third to fourth power of the field.

Conventional low-temperature superconducting tokamaks like ITER operate with on-axis magnetic fields near 5 tesla and peak coil fields around 12 tesla. Roughly doubling those figures—to about 10 to 12 tesla on axis and 20 tesla at the coils, as enabled by high-temperature superconductors like REBCO—boosts fusion power density by roughly a factor of sixteen. Because this scaling is so steep, even a two-fold increase in magnetic field strength can reduce a reactor's required plasma volume by an order of magnitude or more, unlocking far smaller, less expensive tokamaks capable of net energy gain.

Roughly doubling the magnetic field strength is enough to unlock dramatically smaller tokamaks. Because the maximum plasma pressure a magnetic field can confine scales as the square of the field strength ($B^2$), and fusion power density scales with the square of plasma pressure, fusion power density rises with the fourth power of the magnetic field ($B^4$). Doubling the field therefore increases fusion power density by a factor of 16, while also improving energy confinement so a much smaller plasma can still reach net energy gain.

In practice, moving from conventional low-temperature superconductors—like ITER's niobium-tin magnets, which produce about 5.3 tesla at the plasma core (roughly 12 tesla at the coil)—to high-temperature superconductors such as REBCO tapes roughly doubles the field to around 12 tesla at the plasma core (about 20 tesla at the coil), as demonstrated for the SPARC tokamak. That twofold jump in magnetic field lets designers shrink the reactor's plasma volume by more than an order of magnitude—roughly 40 times smaller than ITER—for comparable fusion performance.

answers.answer:
Roughly **twice the magnetic field in the plasma** can make a tokamak dramatically smaller. ITER is designed for 5.3 tesla at the plasma center, while the compact SPARC tokamak is designed for 12.2 tesla, using superconducting coils that reach about 20 tesla at their peak.

The leverage comes from a rule of thumb: at the same plasma temperature and ratio of plasma pressure to magnetic pressure, fusion power per unit volume scales roughly as the fourth power of the field. Doubling the field can therefore yield about 16 times the fusion power per unit volume. How much the whole machine can shrink also depends on confinement, heat exhaust, and shielding.
